title: When Tics and Autism Meet: Phenomenology, Severity, and Treatment Patterns
population: Calgary tertiary pediatric/adult clinic referrals with primary tic disorders; ages 3–72, mean 15.23. Functional, adult-onset and secondary tics excluded. Not an adult-only or severe-adult cohort.
comparator: ASD versus no documented ASD; nonrandomized
exposure: Documented ASD diagnosis; age, sex, comorbidity and current medication covariates
outcomes: Clinician YGTSS past-week tic inventory, total tic score and separately rated tic-related impairment at first visit; recorded comorbidity and prescriptions
follow_up: Analysis uses first visit only despite longitudinal parent registries
results: Exploratory adjusted ASD association: impairment coefficient −4.49 points (95% CI −8.46 to −0.51; p=.027); total tic score coefficient −0.31 (−2.91 to 2.29; p=.814). Unadjusted total severity, impairment and global scores did not differ significantly. Some complex tics and ADHD were more frequent with ASD. Prescription differences are not comparative efficacy.
attrition_missingness: Model counts 483/485 are below total 535; outcome-specific missingness should not be replaced by the enrollment denominator.
risk_of_bias: Cross-sectional tertiary referral sample; residual confounding and treatment-by-indication
Exploratory multiple comparisons; no multiplicity control established
Tic/stereotypy classification and communication/reporting differences can affect impairment ratings
Only three participants had ASD support level 3; severe support-needs applicability limited
funding_conflicts: Registry start-up support: Owerko Centre, Alberta Children’s Hospital Research Institute; article declares no conflicts, with additional author disclosures in supporting material not audited.
applicability: Includes children and adults, but adult-specific estimates not established; lower measured impairment does not establish lower true burden.
related_cohorts: Calgary Child Tic Disorders Clinical Registry
claim_supported: ASD-related differences in measured phenomenology, comorbidity and treatment patterns within this referral sample.
claim_not_supported: No causal ASD effect, treatment benefit, general prevalence, adult-specific estimate, or proof of reduced lived burden.
next_verification_task: Audit age-stratified estimates and measurement/missingness before adult-specific or burden comparisons; do not pool overlapping registry reports without cohort checks.

title: Clinical factors predicting tic persistence into adulthood
population: Adults from earlier TS genetic studies, ages 26–78, mean 44.3; selected responders, predominantly White/non-Hispanic. Original-study exclusions limit intellectual-disability/ASD applicability.
comparator: Within-person recalled childhood/adulthood worst-ever scores and observational between-person covariates; no prospective control
exposure: Recalled childhood severity/impairment, lifetime OCD/ADHD classification, current tic medication and recalled contemporaneous life-event presence
outcomes: Modified self-report YGTSS current six-month, childhood-worst and adult-worst total tic scores and separate impairment; 50 reused current scores as adult-worst
follow_up: Cross-sectional retrospective survey, not prospectively observed childhood-to-adult outcome prediction
results: Table 4 adult-worst severity: childhood-worst coefficient .54 (SE .08); OCD 3.30 (SE 1.39; p=.018). ADHD p=.82 and life-event p=.098 were nonsignificant. Impairment: current medication 4.76 (p=.020), life event 5.00 (p=.0078), childhood-worst .41; OCD printed p=.050 despite significance wording. Do not repair the threshold or infer medication harm.
attrition_missingness: 334/758 responded; 258 retained after completeness/consistency criteria. Model-specific sample sizes and missingness need further audit.
risk_of_bias: Response/selection bias and restricted demographic/diagnostic representation
Data-driven predictor inclusion at p<.1; no external predictive validation
Lifetime OCD described as childhood OCD in discussion; current medication may postdate recalled adult-worst outcome
funding_conflicts: NIH and Rosen Family Foundation support; Scharf reports TAA scientific advisory role/travel support; editor reports past coauthorship.
applicability: Direct evidence about a selected adult sample, not the prevalence of persistence or a universal remission trajectory; sustained severe burden must not be erased by averages.
related_cohorts: Prior Tourette genetics and phenomenology studies; cross-report overlap requires checking before pooling
claim_supported: Associations among recalled tic severity, impairment and comorbid/clinical characteristics in selected adult respondents.
claim_not_supported: No prospective prediction, causal life-event or medication effect, treatment benefit, population persistence/remission estimate, or disease modification.
next_verification_task: Bounded audit of model denominators, missingness and temporal alignment of lifetime OCD/current medication with retrospective worst-ever outcomes; preserve printed p=.050 without threshold repair.
